title: Ed Chi - The Future of Personalized Universal Agents

segments.text: ED H. CHI: Hi, everyone.
Good afternoon.
Last night, I was at the reception and someone told me
that based upon last year's talk, they made a lot of money
in the stock market.
So I don't know if I can make that promise today.
But to be honest, I have a confession to make.
I'm actually a very slow learner.
And I have always felt like I have imposter syndrome.
How many of you have imposter syndrome?
Yeah, me too.
So one of the things I wanted to talk about
is that it took me a long time to figure out what were really
the key ideas that really matter, because as a scientist,
I really cared about was not writing the next paper.
But actually, what the next big idea is.
And in reality, even though I published more than 200 papers,
there's only probably 10 that I feel like are even proud of.
And so I wanted to tell you in retrospect
what I feel like are three very important ideas
from the first two decades of my graduate research career,
and they come from the area of information retrieval.
And these are ideas that many of you have already heard about.
So I'm not going to go into them into detail, obviously.
But the first one, let's just pause and think
about the first great invention of humankind,
in my opinion, which was the library.
And the library actually is built upon the idea of indexing.
And so that was the very first big idea from the 90s,
where we used MapReduce to build very large search engines.
But it needed a second idea, which was vector space models.
And only a few years ago, the word2vec paper was voted
as the 10th year test of time award for word2vec,
and it was based upon the idea of vector space models using
neural networks to compute complete relationship between
words so that we can have better understanding of semantics
and what words really mean.
And those were already two ideas.
And I'm going to tell you the first major mistake
I made as a slow thinker and a slow learner.
In 1992, my PhD advisor, John Riedl, came to me
and said, what if we used those vector space models
and applied them to user-item matrices instead
of document-term matrices.
This was the birth of recommendation systems
and I told him it was a dumb idea.
And the reality was that once we got huge supercomputers,
we were able to do one thing much, much
better as a result that made search and recommendation
systems so much better.
And that was sorting.
The reality is that what we're doing is ranking.
So if you think about the fact that next token prediction is
nothing but sorting to the next most likely word you're
going to say or to communicate, everything
has been about sorting.
So the third idea from the period,
the latter part of 2010 to 2015 is deep neural networks.
And at Google, actually, we made very good use of this
as you can imagine.
But in 1992, when I was graduate student,
this was a supercomputer.
It had 2.6 gigaflops of computation.
The phone in my pocket right now has 1690 gigaflops--
almost 1,000 times more computation.
And all this powers all the applications that's
in your pocket right now.
We're all walking around with 1,000 supercomputers
in our pocket.
Luckily, it's not burning a hole in your pocket.
And so if you think about the whole internet ecosystem,
this is what we're talking about.
This is the whole thing is still based upon sorting and ranking
and recommendation systems and search.
So those were the three ideas from the first two decades
of my research career.
In my opinion, that really matters--
indexing, vector space models, and deep learning.
Now, the interesting thing is that deep learning
is the real thing that connects it to our present time.
There were three ideas from 2015 to 2025,
and I noticed Vincent is here, hopefully agree with me.
That really mattered from those 10 years of time period.
How many of you have seen this figure?
Yeah, everyone's seen them.
Have you ever read it, the paper?
The very first sentence of the abstract says this.
The dominant sequence transduction models
are based upon complex recurrent neural networks that
include an encoder and decoder.
I'll admit to you that the first time I read this paper,
I have no clue what that meant.
How many of you still don't know what that means?
Yeah, that's what I thought.
Almost-- at least 50% of the people raised their hand.
What is sequential transduction?
What the F does that even mean?
It turns out that the word transduction
means the transformation from one energy wave
into another energy wave.
As an example, you're experiencing transduction
right now.
A microphone that I'm wearing right now
is a transducer that transmits, transforms sound waves
into electrical wave.
And there are speakers all around this hall
that turns those electrical waves back into sound.
That's how you're able to hear me.
In fact, your ear is a transducer.
It's listening to what I'm saying.
And that sound is going into your ear,
which has a membrane, and that membrane is vibrating.
And it's connected to a neuron, and that those neurons are
transmitting information into your brain.
That's how we're able to communicate.
That's how you're able to understand what I'm saying.
So the major first idea in 2014 or so
was actually the idea of using sequential transduction
and marry it with neural networks.
It was an incredible idea.
And so it's very important that you
understand we're not just doing sequential transduction
in the ether.
It was based upon a cognitive understanding
of how our brain worked.
That's how we're able to communicate.
That's how we're able to communicate with our computers
at this point.
The amazing thing is that this model,
this new universal computational model,
is able to do convergence.
It's able to take in multi-modality data.
It's able to understand all kinds of different languages
all at the same time.
The second big idea from that 10-year period came from a basic
question that Denny Zhou and I were asking in Google Brain,
which was, can we teach machines the way we teach our children?
It turns out there was a one dominant way in which we
were doing it wrong.
How were we doing it wrong?
When you teach your kids, I hope every time they get it wrong,
you don't just hit them.
But that was the way that we were teaching our machines.
Denny and I thought maybe we should give them an explanation
why they're wrong.
That came out with the idea of chain of thought.
Give them an explanation.
This is how you do it.
And then have them follow the recipe
for how to solve problems.
This is known as top-down processing.
These days in our industry, in my personal opinion,
we actually have way too much bottom-up processing,
particularly using RL, when in fact, we
should be teaching machines the way
that we teach kids with more top-down processing.
Give them explanations.
So if you think about it, how are we
able to distill one model into another?
It's all because of chain of thought, the reasoning traces.
So the emergence of this idea of going from next token prediction
that was enabled by sequential transduction
into next idea prediction using chain of thought
was the key move that started the whole reasoning field.
Now, so in retrospect, I wish we had not called it large language
models.
Rather, we should have been calling them large reasoning
models, because what we really care about
is their ability to reason.
So there were three ideas, therefore,
in 2015 to 2025 that really mattered.
The first one, sequential transduction.
The second one, next idea prediction was chain of thought.
The third one is post-training.
And there are plenty of talks here
on this stage talking to you about how post-training is done
and all the latest advances that's going on there.
Now, what are the emerging ideas in the next 10 years,
from 2025 to 2035 that say?
Well, what if all of this ecosystem
starts to change, for example?
If you didn't realize a single V8 TPU chip,
now it's 4.7 times more computation than the Cray Y-MP
that I showed you at the beginning of the talk, that's
definitely going to burn a hole in your pocket.
And what is it enabling?
Let's take a look at it a short video.
[VIDEO PLAYBACK]
- I get a gift for my friend, and this is
everything she's been reading.
How would you describe her taste and books?
- Based on these titles, your friend
seems to enjoy a mix of history, biography,
and perhaps a touch of political or social commentary.
- I picked some of these out.
Any idea which one she'd like the most?
- Consider Half of a Yellow Sun for its exploration
of complex social and political issues
within a historical setting, aligning with her interest
in narratives that offer insight into significant periods.
[END PLAYBACK]
ED H. CHI: Now, that is not just sorting and ranking anymore,
is it?
That is where personal assistance is going.
Last year when I was on stage here, I showed this slide.
That was more than a year ago.
Now, everybody is talking about agents.
The ideas were already there.
The next ideas of the next decade is already happening.
And Richard just talked about self-improvement, for example.
There have been other speakers that
talk about multi-modality tool use,
multi-step complex reasoning.
My main work at Google at this point
is just focused around reasoning and planning,
because that is where the future is.
Thank you very much.
[APPLAUSE]
